speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not the rule I am making at all. I understood the hon. gentleman again to refer to the charge asi having been made, after the hon. members concerned bad denied it. Under these circumstances, I think the hon. gentleman should accept -their denial, and not persist in repeating the charge.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I bow to your decision. Now, let me state what is appearing in the public press as to the way in which the Department of Railways and Canals has been conducted under hon. gentlemen opposite and Mr. Blair. Surely that is a matter for inquiry by hon. gentlemen opposite. There is a paper in this city called ' Events,' in which on November 26 there appeared most startling statements which are worthy of inquiry by this House or by a Royal Commission. What are these charges :
In passing we might explain how Mr. Russell stole the St. John ' Telegraph.' After a certain political transaction, carried out under the Department of Railways and Canals, $25,000 was put into the St. John ' Telegraph ' stock. A certain contractor put up another $25,000 and a small amount of stock stood in the name of A. G. Blair, $5,000 we believe. The total capital stock of the company was $75,000 and only $69,000 of this had been issued. Mr. Dave Russell bought $9,000 of it, and as the contributors of the $50,000 did not wish their names to be known in eonnection with the subscriptions their stock was given to Mr. Dave Russell to hold in trust, it being, of course the control of the paper which the owners of the $50,000 worth of stock desired to retain. Mr. Russell then proceeded to treat the paper as his own, and when the directors protested he turned them out. He then offered the paper for sale to the Liberals for $125,000. The reason he was enabled to achieve this daring theft of an important daily newspaper was the desire of the two men who had placed their stock in trust with Mr. Russell not to be publicly connected with the affair.
is this the state of political morality in this Dominion to-day-that associated with the Minister of Railways and Canals is this gentleman, Mr. David Russell, of whom I have nothing good or bad to say, because 1 am not in a position to say it; that he stands as an intermediary, a toll-taker, between contractors and the department, that from a certain contractor $25,000 was filched and was used to purchase stock in a newspaper, that the deal was put through by Mr. Russell, and that by it he cleared no less than $125,000. The ministers cannot ignore these charges which are going through the country, nor turn a deaf ear to them when they hear them in this House. The public will expect, after the charges are stated in this House, that the same shall be fully investigated. This paper goes on to say :
Why was Mr. Russell so anxious to have the nominating of Mr. Blair's successor in the Department of Railways and Canals ? The answer Mr. BENNETT.
to this auestion is Abbey's Salts. Mr. Russell formed a partnership of some sort with Mr. Blair on the salts business. During the past three or four years Mr. Blair made about $80,000 out of it. Mr. Russell no doubt made much more, for Mr. Russell is clever. How ? For some years no dividend has been declared on .the stock. Promises have been given but nothing more. Mr. Russell is an adept at promises. In the meantime every contractor under the Department of Railways and Canals was expected to take a few thousands of stock in Abbey's Salts.
What paper is that in ?

The ' Events ' of November 26. It cannot be pretended that the government are not aware of that charge made by a Liberal journal in this city. Is it not then high time that they should announce that there will he an investigation into everything done in that department while Mr. Blair was at its head. But if you rule, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot go into these other matters by giving quotations from public newspapers connecting the names of ministers in connection with attempts made to bribe them by contractors, I must of course bow to your ruling. But the question discussed in this newspaper is surely worthy the consideration of the first minister. Surely he is not going to do what Mr. Ross did in the Ontario House when the Sullivan, Stratton, Gamey, investigation was up. What happened then ? For three hours Mr. Stratton was accused of all kinds of crimes, and after these three hours of accusation, Mr, Ross stood up in his place and said that the next day Mr. Stratton' would reply. That was certainly not an evidence of innocence, and I hope that the right hon. the first minis ter will go further than Mr. Stratton din and announce that there will be a full investigation into the conduct of the Department of Railways and Canals as regards this very matter. Let us go a little further. Tt was stated in the papers-and I suppose no one will rise to take Mr. Blair's part, because evidently there is none so poor as to do him reverence-that Mr. Blair was to take the stump. Perhaps the right lion, gentleman will explain why he did not. That is a matter concerning which the "House and the country desire an explanation and which is worthy of investigation. But the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) made this afternoon a very savage attack against Mr. R. L. Borden, and I think, in Mr. Borden's absence, it is only fair that I should place on ' Hansard ' the statement he made on the subject in connection with which the hon. gentleman made the charge he did.

I would beg to inform the hon. gentleman again that I never mentioned Mr. Borden's name or referred to him in any way this afternoon, and I shall leave to the unrevised ' Hansard ' the proof of mv statement.
Who then did the hon. gentleman give as his authority for the statement that Mr. Blair was to be taken into the cabinet to be formed by Mr. Borden 1
I do not propose to give my authority just now. The hon. gentleman will know it soon enough. We are not going to show our hand just now.

Then I presume the hon. gentleman is speaking on behalf of the government and there is after all going to be an investigation. If the right hon. the First Minister will say that there will be an inquiry, that will put an end to my remarks. 'But the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) had something to say with regard to this matter in an interview which he gave the Montreal ' Herald ; ' and in that interview he certainly placed Mr. Borden in rather an unenviable light. On December 5, he gave the Montreal ' Herald ' this statement with reference to Mr. R. L. Borden :
I have no hesitation in telling you all I know about it,' said Mr. Emmerson. I was in New York on the 18th of September, and a gentleman approached me at the hotel I was staying at and asked me if there was no chance of getting a contract for the construction of the transcontinental railway. The elections, be said, were coming off, and if a contract was obtained there would be lots of money to swell the campaign fund. I told him that the work *would have to be done by Canadian contractors, and refused to have anything to do with him.
Ho told me that they were working through Montreal people and I knew afterwards that Montreal parties acted very suddenly and peculiarly during the campaign. At the hotel was J. N. Greenshields, of Montreal. The Montreal people were said to be friends of David Russell. During the elections David Russell, J. N. Green-shields, two Americans, Dr. Kennedy and a Mr. Green, said to be an Englishman, who resided in the States for some years, visited my province.
They were riding in a magnificent private car and at Fredericton Junction on October 22, met Mr. R. L. Borden, apparently by appointment. Mr. Borden went on board, having been met at the station by Mr. Dowling, private secretary of Mr. David Russell. During the run' to St. John, Mr. Borden, Mr. Greenshields and others were closeted together.
In the province of Quebec ' La Presse ' was captured. But this was only preliminary work. There was, so I am told, to be on nomination day some twenty-five Liberal members who would retire. In this way twenty-five Conservatives would be elected in that province by acclamation. and this would secure the return of the Conservatives, when R. L. Borden would have charge of the construction of the transcontinental line and the giving out of the contracts. In connection with the resignation of Mr. Blair it may be mentioned that four days afterwards there appeared in a New York financial paper that he was to be the head of a syndicate for which the capital had been secured to control the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific. But something went wrong, and the plan of campaign fell through. ' That, said Mr. Emmerson, ' is what I know and what I have heard about it'.
IS}	.
If that is a correct report of Mr. Emmer-son's statement-and I am not aware that he has contradicted it-he cast a reflection on twenty-five gentlemen who presumably have seats in this House from the province of Quebec ; and every hon. member from that province, in justice to himself, should demand from the government a full investigation and have the doubt cleared up whether or not they were parties to the infamous scheme by which they were to destroy this government, if at all possible, and had agreed to do this for a monetary consideration. I shall be very much surprised indeed if some hon. gentlemen from the province of Quebec do not demand a full and thorough investigation. But we have a further statement from another gentleman rather friendly to the government. I refer to the Speaker of the Senate. He said :
I heard ou nomination day that the bombshell of the Tories was to develop as follows : [DOT] The Tories, having secured the ' Presse,' were to keep the fact of having done so carefully from the public knowledge, and on nomination day Mr. Blair was to make extraordinary revelations. On the same day two or three ministers of the Crown were to be arrested for malfeasance in office. The next day the ' Presse ' was to denounce the government and ask all honest men to turn out the Laurier government because of the revelations made by Mr. Blair. A certain number-as many as they could secure -of the Liberal candidates were to resign in disgust and allow as many Conservatives to be returned by acclamation.
Naturally Mr. Speaker Dandurand did not wish to make a wholesale accusation against the Liberal members from Quebec, and consequently did not state the number. Here then we have a statement made by a minister of the Crown and another made by the Speaker of the Senate, both published in a Liberal newspaper, and surely these are worthy of investigation. Then it is asked why did not the scheme succeed, and one newspaper thus answered that question.
The generally accepted theory is that the premier secured information which Mr. Blair was unwilling to have made public, and obtained it from Mr. Lambert Payne, formerly private secretary to Mr. Blair, and now to Mr. Emmerson.
What does that mean ? It is a statement in effect that Mr. Payne whilst secretary to Mr. Blair, became aware of certain actions in the department and had communicated these to Mr. Emmerson, and that the threat on the part of the first minister to expose Mr. Blair's conduct was sufficient to prevent his going on the public platform and making the expected denunciation.
Now, I desire to be perfectly fair and will add that I have seen in the public press an explicit denial by Mr. Payne, who is personnally known to many hon. members, especially to the older members,-and every one who knows him will accept his explanation that he in no way was a party to an exposure of Mr. Blair. There is the

matter as it is to-day before the public, set fortli in tbe newspapers in the most positive and public manner, set forth in newspapers favourable to hon. gentlemen opposite and referred to in statements made by ministers of the Crown who were associated with the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Em-mersou). The stories have been rife for a year or two that the Minister of Railways and Canals was the object of a plot to effect his downfall. And it may be that the Minister of Railways and Canals has set broadcast these statements relative to other ministers with the hope of defeating or at least of injuring them. I do hope that some hon. gentleman on that side, clothed with authority and knowledge-and that would mean that it must be none other thau the Prime Minister himself-will rise in his place and state positively that there shall be and will be a thorough, a complete, a searching investigation of the whole matter. Ret that investigation be by any authority that is competent, whether by a commission, as hon. gentlemen opposite seem to prefer, or by a committee of this House. In that connection, perhaps the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) knows whereof he speaks, because I notice that he is chairman of the Committee on Privileges and Elections. But, in view of the hon. gentleman's action in presenting himself as a would-be voter in the city of Ottawa, where he must have known that he was not entitled to vote-and I have heard no denial from him of this statement which has been repeated here-it is about time for the Prime Minister to ask him to withdraw from the chairmanship of that committee. In reference to the part played by Mr. R. L. Borden in this matter, I think it only fair in his absence to place on ' Hansard ' the statement made by him, under date of Dec. Oth he gave this interview in Montreal :
With reference to certain press statements respecting Mr. Blair's resignation as chairman of the Railway Commission, I wish to say that that resignation came as a great surprise to me. I did not directly or indirectly suggest to him or ask him to resign. I held out no inducement to him to resign. I had no interview with him upon the subject, nor did any one on my behalf approach him upon the subject. In short I had nothing whatever to do with his resignation, and I was thoroughly surprised -when I heard of it.
I had no connection with and I knew nothing of any negotiations respecting the alleged change of ownership of ' La Presse,' and I had nothing to do with such change, if it took place. I never had any interview or communication with any English or American capitalists, or with any other person, with respect to any proposed contracts for the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I never even heard of the alleged construction syndicate. No one approached me with any proposal respecting the construction of that railway. Any statement or suggestion to the contrary is utterly without foundation.
I never received any contribution for any purpose from Mr. Russell or Mr. Greenshields or Mr. BENNETT. -
any gentleman connected with them, or from any English or American capitalists, nor did the Conservative party, so far as I am aware. Until the article in the ' Toronto World ' appeared I had never even heard of any attempt by Conservatives to induce the withdrawal of Liberal candidates in the province of Quebec. It would astonish me beyond measure to learn that any such attempt was made or proposed.
Now, this question is before the House, and to-morrow's newspapers will place it before tbe country. And, while the government are strong in this House, while it is clear from the applause that greets every statement of the ministerial benches whether creditable or discreditable, it is evident that this government cannot he defeated in this House. Judging by that applause I cannot conceive that it would be possible to force the greater part of these who sit behind tbe ministers to vote against this government, no matter how odious or nefarious any act of theirs may be.
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think tbe hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) should retract that statement.
Oh, very well : I withdraw it. As I cannot repeat that statement here I can only repeat it in other places, and t expect to do so on many occasions.
Withdraw.

I have gone through the province of Ontario, or parts of it within the last month, and have addressed many public audiences. And, I care not what public opinion in other provinces may be, I can tell the Prime Minister here to-night, that, unless an inquiry is made into the matter we have been discussing, public opinion m tbe great province of Ontario will be stronger against him even than it was on the 3rd of November last. I do not wish to harrow up the feelings of hon. gentlemen who had a trial of-strength in the province of Ontario lately, and they know the result. The whole corps of officials and all the power and influence of this government were joined to those of the provincial government, and what was the result ? I need not harrow up the feeling of hon. gentlemen opposite by referring to the matter at length. They know that, against all the power of this government and of the local government, and against all the power of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which carried free not only hundreds but thousands of voters who were expected to vote for tbe Liberals, this government received, in the great province of Ontario a rebuke that did not well please the Prime Minister and that to-day saddens him to recall. And another thing that he recalls with pain is that the old Liberal county of Huntingdon, for the first time in its history, went Conservative under the rule of the present Prime Minister of this Dominion.

At the risk of prolonging this discussion which, perhaps, has already been prolonged too much, I desire to offer a few observations. Those observations will not be lengthy so far as they concern the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) who has just taken his seat. He has played again the role with which he lias made us familiar in past sessions in this House when he bandies about the names of ministers and prominent members on this side. I say to him and to those on his side of the House, that if he has any charge to make against any of the ministers whom he has been pleased to name, there is a proper way for him to present that charge. I will challenge him, I will dare him. to stand in his place and make a single charge against any hon. gentleman on this side, and I will give him the floor if he desires to speak. He has mentioned the name c.f the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prgfontaine). Is he prepared to make a charge against that gentleman ? He has mentioned the Minister of Justice (Mr-Fitzpatrick). Is he prepared to make a charge against the Minister of Justice ? No, he is not. He is doing what we have seen him do in this House many a time before, using the names of men occupying prominent and responsible positions in this country, but not daring to make a charge against them. There is a proper course and an improper course in these matters, and the hon. gentleman has seen fit to take the improper course.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. A. Johnston) wish me to answer ?
I do.

I can tell the hon. gentleman that I have been elected to this House for four parliaments. My last majority was 383 and my smallest was 32. And, if the reputation of this government in Ontario goes as it has been going, my majority next time will be six hundred.

There, Mr. Speaker, is the same old story. I have been good enough to give the hon. gentleman an opportunity to justify the statements he has made. I am still prepared to give way to him if he is ready to make a charge against any member of this House. Let me repeat that he has seen fit on this occasion, as on former occasions, to adopt the improper course when he chooses to address the members of this House of Commons. All I have to say on this occasion is that the coward and the slanderer is abroad in this country.
Order.
I do not mean "to say that the hon. gentleman is one.

I rise to a point of order. I ask the ruling of the Speaker whether
such language is permissible, because it evidently refers to the hon. gentleman ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The term would have been objectionable if persisted in, but the hon. gentleman at once stated that he did not propose to apply it to the hon. gentle* man (Mr. Bennett). Otherwise the term would have been out of order.

Understand me, well, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to make that observation apply to any member occupying a seat in this House ; but I do say again that the coward and the slanderer is abroad in this country, and the sooner he is picked out and his picture held up to the people of this country, the better it will be for the country. Sir, I hope, and I am sure hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House will share that hope, that when hon. members venture to make insinuations of a very unsavory character with respect to members occupying seats in this House, if they have any charge to make, the proper thing for them to do is to make it. I will not pursue this subject any further. Now, why did Mr. Blair resign the chairmanship of the Railway Commission ? That is the question.
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman says, Hear, hear. I have no doubt that if he applied to hon. gentlemen occupying prominent positions in his own party he would be told very quickly the reasons why Mr, Blair resigned from the chairmanship of the Railway Commission. I propose, before I sit down, to call witnesses in this House on that matter, witnesses whom the hon. gentleman will be compelled to admit occupy prominent positions in the councils of the party of which be is a member. I propose to call as witness the ' Mail and Empire,' and I propose to call a greater witness still, the Montreal ' Star,' which conducted the campaign on behalf of the Conservative party which ended on the 3rd of November last. It was the leading organ of the Conservative party. I wonder why my hon. friend, who is anxious to know why Mr. Blair resigned, does not ask Mr. Hugh Graham, proprietor of the Montreal ' Star,' why Mr. Blair resigned. I am quite sure he would be told why. Is it not notorious all over this land that Mr. Graham was the one person perhaps in this country who was possessed of the information before it was announced to the public, that Mr. Blair was about to resign his position as chairman of the Railway Commission ? True it is that Mr. David Russell, who was one of the stalwarts of the Conservative party during the last campaign, has told us over and over again that he induced Mr. Blair to resign. He tells us so himself. Mr. Hugh Graham also tells the people of this country that he knew Mr. Blair was going to resign. Now, I have selected a few extracts at random from Conservative papers of about

the date of the resignation ; as nearly as I can find out, it occurred on the 18th or 19th of October last. I have mentioned the Montreal ' Star ' as the leading organ of the Conservative party in the Dominion of Canada. Some people may take exception to that, but I think any hon. gentleman in this House who followed the history of the Conservative party during the past three or four years can reach no other conclusion than that the Montreal ' Star ' was, during that time, the organ which was more intimately associated with the Conservative party than any other newspaper in this country. Now, we find a despatch from St. John, New Brunswick, in the Montreal ' Star ' of October 19, and what does it say ?
To-day there is no other topic on the street. Conservatives are jubilant, Liberals dumbfounded.
My hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean), at an early stage of this debate, said that he was ashamed of the conduct of the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, Mr. Blair, in resigning his position on the Railway Commission. He was ashamed of it; but the Conservatives in the city of St. John were jubilant because of it, and the Conservatives in every other city in the Dominion of Canada were jubilant. My hon. friend from South York was alone among the Conservatives who was ashamed, as nearly as we can find out, of the action of the ex-Minister of Railways in resigning his seat on that board. The St. John ' Telegraph,' of which we heard so much, and which was quoted at great length in the campaign in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick-the St. John ' Telegraph ' said
The resignation of Mr. Blair at this time, and the announcement which accompanies it will lend new force and depth to the swelling tide of popular feeling which animates this great country to-day, and which the government is ignoring to its peril and to its undoing.
The government was ignorant according to this paper. Then the St. John ' Sun,' which is a leading organ of the Conservative party in the province of New Brunswick, has this to say :
It is useless to suggest that Mr. Blair's resignation has no political significance. Its chief public significance is political. Mr. Blair is too old and experienced a politician not to understand the effect of his resignation at this stage of the campaign. If he were retiring for purely private or professional reasons-
The St. John ' Sun,' the leading organ of the Conservative party in New Brunswick, knew at that time that Mr. Blair was not resigning for purely private or professional reasons. What then was he resigning for 1 The leading organ of the Conservative party in New Brunswick evidently knew why he resigned. Why don't they tell us ? Why don't they take hon. gentlemen opposite into their confidence, if they are so anxious to ascertain why it was that he resigned ?

The evidence is clear and distinct that they were aware of the reasons.
If he were retiring for purely private or professional reasons he would wait longer, as the premier must strongly desire him to do. But if Mr. Blair desires to strike one more blow at the project which he has declared to be full of peril to the nation, he knows that this is his great chance-his last one.
That is what they say. Then the St. John ' Star,' another leading organ of the Conservative party in New Brunswick and the Dominion of Canada, said :
The weight of his fighting ability and his influence thrown with the Conservative campaign against that policy

That is against the policy of the government.

against that policy at this time renders even more certain than it seemed yesterday the triumph of the policy of the people.
That is, the policy of the Conservative party, so-called. My hon. friend from South York is ashamed of the conduct of the exchairman of the Railway Commission ; the leading organs of the party of which he is a member are heartily proud of the conduct of Mr. Blair. Then there is the ' Citizen,' the leading organ of the Conservative party in the city of Ottawa. It says :
The people believe that these personal sacrifices have been prompted by patriotic motives, and that belief has stimulated the expectation that a man of Mr. Blair's acknowledged political power and weight in national life will not remain satisfied with a mere personal protest'; that his sense of obligation to the people will force him to come forward and make the consummation of this ruinous deal an impossibility.
That Is the opinion of the Ottawa 1 Citizen,' and yet my hon. friend from South York is ashamed of the conduct of Mr. Blair. Then there is the ' Mail and Empire.' Surely it will not be denied that this paper occupies a prominent position in the councils Of the Conservative party ? What does it say ?
The incident is highly dramatic.
Highly dramatic, of course.
Here is a public man commanding the highest position in the gift of the government-. In this office he might have remained for the remainder of his natural life. But a great issue is before us-an issue in respect of which he is well informed-and he lays aside his appointment and his emoluments in order that Canada may again be warned of the danger that lurks in the proposition we are now asked to endorse.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are anxious to ascertain why it was that Mr. Blair resigned. Why do they not read the 'Mail and Empire' in order to- be perfectly informed as to his reasons for resigning. Now there are several other statements that might be called in evidence to give this country an idea as to the reasons for Mr. Blair's resignation. We might appeal to the evidence of those hon.

gentlemen of the Conservative party wlio pressed Mr. Blair with invitations to speak for them all over the country. Who are the gentlemen, who, according to the Montreal 1 Star,' pressed him to speak in the city of Toronto ? Did any hon. gentlemen from the city of Toronto do so ? They pressed him to speak at Kingston, London, Brock-ville, Peterboro, Hamilton, Windsor, Chatham, St. Thomas, Niagara, St. Catharines, Quebec, Montreal, Three Rivers, St. John, Halifax, Moncton, Sussex, Fredericton, Amherst, Truro, Pictou and my own city of Sydney.
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. A. Johnston) means to say that the Conservative party in the city or county of St. John asked Mr. Blair to speak during the election he is entirely mistaken.

I am simply, Mr. Speaker, giving the House the benefit of tne information given the country and the public and which has been generally supplied to them by the leading organ of the Conservative party, the Montreal * Star.'

I am giving a denial of that statement, Mr. Speaker, and according to the ruling you made in respect to the hon. gentleman in front of me, that denial should be accepted. The statement is absolutely untrue.

I accept without any reservation whatever the denial made by my hon. friend (Mr. Stockton), but I want to point out to him that it is not a denial of any statement made by me. It is a denial of a statement made by the leading organ of the party of which he is a member.

Mr. Speaker, I desire, as one of the representatives of the city of Hamilton, to give an equally explicit denial of the statement in regard to that city. There was no request whatever to Mr. Blair to deliver any speech at Hamilton.

I accept with equal cordiality the statement made by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) and it is another evidence of the unreliability of the statements that were handed out to the people of this country by this great organ of public opinion.

Mr. Speaker, I desire on behalf of my own constituency of St. John to make a denial similar to the one already made by my hon. colleague from the county (Mr. Stockton). The Conservative party in St. John made no attempt whatever to obtain the services of Mr. Blair or to induce him to deliver an address in the city of St. John.

I accept again, as I have accepted in the case of the hon. gentlemen who have preceded him, the denial of my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel). I followed the addresses delivered in the city of St.
John somewhat closely during the campaign, I followed the addresses made by my hon. friend in his own campaign, and I did not notice during the progress of that campaign that he or his colleagues took any exception to the very many remarkable things that were said by members of the Conservative party, of Mr. Blair. I think he fully concurred in everything which was said about him owing to the benefits that were going to accrue to the Conservative party as a result of his conduct, and I think he was prepared to accept the full benefit that he expected would accrue to the Conservative party. A great many people in the hon. gentleman's own party will not hesitate to say that were it not for the position assumed by Mr. Blair in this country neither himself nor his colleague would have been elected.
Mr. Speaker, I desire you to read the resolution before the House. I fail to see the connection between the hon. gentleman's remarks and the resolution.
Mr. Speaker
I think I am quite wdthin my right in asking you, Mr. Speaker, to read the resolution.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite within his right in asking to have the resolution read at any stage of the debate.
Not during a speech.
At any time. I understand it is my right.
You cannot interrupt an hon. member.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: My recollection of the rule is that a request may be made at any time to read the resolution before the House. If the hon. gentleman desires to have the resolution read. I will read it.
I have no desire to impose upon you, Mr. Speaker, the reading of this resolution, but I do not want to sit here and be imposed upon by a gentleman discussing a question which is not before the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If it was not the desire of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) to have the resolution read, I do not think he should have asked to have it read.
I would ask you to read It unless the hon. gentleman is called to order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think there has been a good deal of latitude allowed in this debate on both sides. The hon. gentleman's remarks are perhaps somewhat irrelevant to the question, but there has been a good deal of latitude and I do not propose to call him any more strictly to account just at present.

I will be delighted to conform myself, Mr. Speaker, to any ruing you may make. My only apology for participating- In this discussion is that I am simply following the lead of lion, gentlemen on the other side of the House. I think that the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) is perhaps more than anybody else responsible for the tux-n which this debate has taken.
ilr. W. F. MACLEAN. In what way ? You had better shelter yourself under some one else on the other side. I do not care to take the responsibility.

It is interesting, however, to have from hon. gentlemen opposite, even at this late date, a contradiction of the reports which were sent out bv this great organ of the public, the Montreal '*Star.' I think, however, Mr. Speaker, it would have been a little better if these lion, gentlemen had risen in their places previously to November 3, last, and repudiated the utterances of this journal. They are willing to do it to-day, but they were not so ready to do it previously to November 3 last. However, I am quite prepared to accept their statements. My hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan), when addressing the House befox-e six o'clock, made reference to the-rumour set abroad in this country that Mr. Blair, in the event of the Conservative party coming into power was going to be a member of the next Conservative cabinet, j Whether or not there was anything in the rumour, I do not know. I am not going to say I attached vei-y much importance to that rumour, but I am here to assert with my hon. friend from Cumberland that there wras such a rumour abroad and I am going to give the House a little bit of evidence just to point out that there was some reason for the faith that was in some people in this country. The Montreal ' Star ' of October 25, had the following :
It' is now stated that after the election a splendid banquet will be given Hon. Mr. Blair in Windsor hotel in recognition of his great public services and his efforts to save the country from the disastrous effects of the government's Grand Trunk Pacific policy. The banquet which will be held on or about November 26th will be, it is stated, the most magnificent function of the kind ever held in Canada.
