Of coui-se, the Montreal ' Star ' may be wi-ong again. Now it is

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
highly probable, in view of the repudiation of hon. gentlemen opposite to-night, that the Montreal 'Star' was wrong again, and therefore it is that I am quite satisfied to allow the matter to drop. My hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Macleau) is ashamed or the conduct of the ex-chairman of the Railway Commision. What does his leader, the leader of the Conservative party say witii regard to this matter ? Speaking at *Sherbi-ooke in the province of Quebec, the night following the announcement of Jit". Blair's retirement, Mr. Borden said :
I at one time like many of you here thought Mr. Blair mercenary, but now I admire him because he has been able to rise to the occasion to say ' although I have the salary, it is my country first.' He had exposed the Laurier government. He has shown the inner workings of their policy.
That does not compare with the opinion which the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. E. Maclean) has of Mr. Blair.
Why did Mr. Blair resign ? That is a question which has been asked us frequently from tlie other side of the House this afternoon. The Montreal ' Star ' of October 21 reports a speech delivered by Mr. Borden, at Woodstock, in the province of New Brunswick. The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has assux-ed this House that Mr. Borden knew nothing whatever about the movements of Mr. Biair. I accept the statemexit of the hoxx. member for Simcoe that Mr. Borden did xxot know, but if you read the x-eport of his speech at Woodstock, as it appears in the ' Star ', you will find this paragraph :
Some one in the audience interrupted at this stage by saying : ' Emmerson will talk about Mr. Blair tomorrow night.'
Like a flash Mr. Borden replied : ' I think the amusing part will be when Mr. Blair comes to talk about Mr. Emmerson.'
Evidently Mr. Borden expected that Mr. Blair was going to take a part in the campaign. Of course we are assured by hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the House that he knew nothixxg about It, and I for my part am prepared to accept that explanation-it is another repudiation by hon. gentlemen opposite of the Montreal ' Star.' I have to apologize to the House for having perhaps transgressed the rules, but I have given my reasons for this transgression. It is somewhat comforting to us on this side that hon. gentlemen have nothing whatever to offer in oppositioxx to the resolution now befox-e the House. The gov-vernment have proposed to the people of this country the appointment of a certain gentleman as chairman of tlxe Railway Commission. Hon. gentlemen opposite have risen one after axxother vying with each other as to which would say the kindest things of the gentleman the government propose to appoint. It is naturally comforting to those of us who sit on the back

benches supporting the government, to know that the appointment they propose making to an important position is one that commends itself to the best judgment of gentlemen who sit not alone on this side of the House but on the opposite side as well.

Mr. Speaker, it was said by one of the Conservative members the other day that criticism is the life of parliament. I should think it is equally true that too much criticism causes sessions of parliament to live unnecessarily long and I should think that a great deal of the criticism of to-night has been wide of the mark. I sympathize with some of the remarks made to-night by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) especially when he stated that he did not think it likely that the reform government would he defeated by the votes of members of this House. I think he is perhaps in that regard deserving of some sympathy. I have wondered if this is where the shoe pinches and if this is at the bottom of the whole trouble. I also learned that the hon. member for East Simcoe marvelled that 25 Reform candidates refused to be bribed, refused to be bought and to play the traitor for the thousands of dollars that had been raised in the effort to bribe them to defeat the Laurier government. That is what I would have expected of 25 Reform candidates in the Dominion of Canada. I would expect they would refuse as they did, to be bought and bribed, preferring to preserve their good consciences and honour. I trust that had the same offer of a bribe been made to Conservative candidates, they would have resisted and refused in the same manner.
There is a vacancy in the chairmanship of the Railway Commission, and I believe the desire of the government is to fill that vacancy with a man well qualified to discharge the duties. I believe that is the desire of the people of this country. I hope that is the desire of the Conservative members of this House. I am glad to hear every one on Either side who has spoken, express the highest opinion of the hon. Mr. Justice Killam. Every one seems to admit that he is a man of integrity and ability and the proper man to fill the position. The hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has said that there has been bargaining and he regrets that there has been bargaining. Sir, it is oftentimes necessary to bargain to obtain the services of a good man. It is never necessary to bargain to obtain the services of an indifferent, poor or incapable man. The acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Foster) has said that the services of Mr. Killam have been obtained upon the lowest terms. If that be true, that a man who is thoroughly capable, a man of the greatest integrity, has been arranged with, and that a bargain
has been made whereby his services have been procured for the people, for the payment of the lowest price, then I should think the interest of the people of this country have been well and truly looked after and I believe the people will be thoroughly satisfied with the arrangement that has been made.

These resolutions are to affect one particular case, they have covered one case which is probably an exception. No objection has been made, I do not think any objection could be made to the gentleman who has been named and who is being provided for in this resolution. Where I think the mistake has been made and where I think the government will be wise in changing this resolution is that they are providing not for this case alone but are making a general Act covering possibilities. Now if the gentleman who is named is appointed, we all hope that he will hold that position for very many years. Ten years or a longer time we hope will elapse before the necessity again arises of appointing a chairman of the Railway Commission. When that period arrives, it is in my judgment very unlikely that a judge of one of the superior courts will be again called upon to fill the position. But if that should- happen ten years hence, it would be a very easy thing to provide for it by a special Act, as is being done in this case, and I think that would do away with all the objection there is to these resolutions. You are putting on the statute-book a law which will naturally be looked to by the judges of the court as containing one of the prizes that will possibly fall to them. I do not think that is necessary or wise ; it is not the proper position in which to place the judges. Let us deal with the one case before us that requires to be dealt with, and confine the resolutions to this particular case, and I believe every one will agree to them.

Before you put the question, Mr. Speaker, will you allow me to make a personal explanation ? On two or three occasions this evening reference has been made to my having offered to vote at the recent provincial election in the city of Ottawa, and, if you will allow me, 1 will state the facts. I happened to be a householder in this city, and as such my name was placed upon the assessment roll, and tor that reason, I believe, was also placed upon the voter's list. I knew nothing about it, however, until a day or two before the provincial election, when I received a notice to the effect that my name was on the provincial voters' list, and asking me to vote at a certain poll. In the province of Nova Scotia, from which I come, if a man's name is on the list, having got. there from the assessment roll, it matters not in a provincial election whether he lives in Nova Scotia or British Columbia, he has a vote. I am

now informed that the same is the case in Manitoba and Quebec. I did not give the matter any consideration ; but knowing that that was the law in Nova Scotia, it never occurred to me that I had not a right to vote in the province of Ontario. Therefore I went to the poll to exercise my franchise, as X thought I had the right to do ; and I am informed to-day by an eminent Ontario lawyer in this House that I had a right to vote. Whether I had or not, X thought I had, as I would have had under the law of Nova Scotia. But having been asked at the poll if I had been a resident of the province of Ontario for a certain length of time, I said I had not; and when it was pointed out to me that there was a residence qualification in this province, I withdrew. I make this explanation to show that there was no wrong intention on my part in this matter.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee.
On resolution 1,
1. Resolved, That if a judge of auy Superior Court in Canada is appointed chief commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada he shall not he removed at any time hy the Governor in Council except upon address of the Senate and House of Commons.

X have not taken any part in this debate, and I do not intend to occupy the attention of the committee at any length now. This is somewhat special legislation. I am not objecting to tin provision of the statute that the appointee shall be removable only upon an address of the two houses of parliament; but I do object to a distinction being made between an appointee who is not a judge and one who is a judge. I think for fair legislation that it is worthy of the consideration of the Minister of Justice to make the law applicable equally to all appointees.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The suggestion which my hon. friend has just made is one that would naturally commend itself at first sight to any intelligent observer of what is going on. But let me point out to my hon. friend the conditions under which this legislation is introduced. It is found necessary to choose the man who above all men we deem to be the best qualified for this particular position. I think my hon. friend, with the knowledge he has of the profession, will come to the conclusion that the gentleman we have in our mind for this position is eminently well qualified to fill it.
I think that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That opinion, I think, is concurred in by all those who have spoken in this debate. It has been suggested hy the present leader of the opposition that something in the nature of a bargain was made between the government and this judge, and in the way he put it such a Mr. LOGAN.
bargain would be in the last degree objectionable. I for my part heartily concur in all that has been said here to-day with respect to the necessity of keeping our judges free from all political entanglements.
1 am a firm believer in the doctrine of once a puisne always a puisne, although, as my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart) observed to-day, that doctrine has been more honoured - in breach than the observance. My hon. friend knows that it has been set at defiance not only in this country, but quite recently in England, in the appointment of the present Lord Chief Justice, Lqrd Alverstone, who was previously Master of the Rolls. It was also set at defiance in the appointment of Lord Russell as Lord Chief Justice of England, he having been Justice of Appeal when appointed. And my hon. friend will remember the discussion which took place in the House of Commons in England in 1872, with respect to the appointment of Sir Robert Collier to the Judicial Committee.
But I think that was universally condemned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend will remember that marvellous letter of Lord Coleridge to the Lord Chancellor, in which he castigated the Lord Chancellor to such an extent that he had shortly afterwards to resign. What was the principle he contended for ? It was the principle, practically consecrated by vote of the Commons of England when, on a motion of censure, Mr. Gladstone was almost defeated as a result of the appointment. What was the principle ? It was that a judge should not be appointed to the highest court of appeal until he had some experience in a lower court. The principle then of once a puisne judge always a puisne judge was formally condemned. I have expressed my opinion-* and it may be considered presumptious in me to have an opinion after what I have quoted-but I would, if I could, have inscribed over the entry to the judicial bench these words : ' Those who enter here leave all hopes of preferment behind.' That is my own view, but that is" not the view which has been adopted. But, after all, one swallow does not make a summer, and it is not because I hold that view against the opinion of the people at large that my opinion should prevail. But let me answer something that fell from my hon. friend the leader of the opposition some few minutes ago. When he noticed how thin was the ice on which the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) was skating, he found it necessary to depart from the principle that his hon. friend was contending for, and he said, with that capacity for refining and making nice distinctions which is so characteristic of his analytical mind : I admit that in principle, preferment in order of promotion on the bench is all right, but when you come to take a man from the bench and

appoint him to a position elsewhere, that is What X object to.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But here again we have a number of precedents. Let me remind my hon. friend of the case quoted by the First Minister, the case of Sir John Thompson, who was taken from the bench and made Minister of Justice in the government of Sir John Macdonald. Let me remind him also of the case of Mr. Angers, who was taken from the judicial bench in my own province and made Lieutenant Governor, and also a case in my own family, which occurred in 1873, when a gentleman was taken from the bench in the province of Quebec and made Lieutenant Governor. These are all eases in which was followed the rule adopted in the present instance. But let me get down to the case in hand. Let me point out to the committee the conditions under which this appointment was made. The government was casting about for a man to replace Mr. Blair.
I am not objecting to tjhe appointment. '

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not speaking to my hon. friend, but at the committee. When we were casting about for a proper person for this position, the man upon whom we fixed our mind was Mr. 'Justice Killam. He was approached and asked if he would accept. His answer was : Here I am now on the bench. I have served on the bench for twenty years. Ten years hence I shall have the right to retire with my full salary. I am now fifty-five years of age, and in addition to that I occupy a position from which I cannot be removed except upon an address from both Houses of parliament. Why should I give up that fixity of tenure in the office I hold and the advantages which will come to me as the result of my occupation of that office with respect to my retiring allowance, to take this position that you offer me ?
For the $30,000 extra he will get.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Allow me. That was his argument. He said: I have an acquired right to my position and the emoluments which will come to me at the time of my retirement. And we thought that was perfectly reasonable, and that we should not in any way interfere with the fixity of his tenure of office or his right to his retiring-allowance at the expiration of his period of office. And this legislation is intended for nothing else than to enable us to give him that position under these conditions. There [DOT]was no other bargain ; and if that can be considered an ill-advised bargain, of course we are responsible for it, and perhaps I am responsible in a larger manner than any one else. But that is the extent of the bargain,
and it does seem to me there is nothing extraordinary in it.

The hon. gentleman is evading the whole question. This resolution says :
That if a judge of any Superior Court in Canada is appointed chief commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada he shall not be removed at any time by the Governor in Council except upon address of the Senate and House of Commons.
The people were given a solemn pledge that the chairman of the Railway Commission would be removable by the Governor in Council and that his conduct could be discussed and criticised in this House. Now, however, the whole scheme is changed, and an effort is made to put an irresponsible man in that position-irresponsible as compared with the chairman under the present law. The whole argument of Mr. Blair, who introduced the Bill, and who was then a colleague of the hon. Minister of Justice, and who was sustained during the whole of the debate by his colleague, was that the chairman and every other member of the commission should be subject to removal by the Governor in Council. In that way he was to be responsible to the government and this House, and could be removed if he failed to do his duty. Now that position is reversed, and nobody is given any authority to compel him to perform his duties. What are his powers? The hon. gentleman read this afternoon what the powers of that commission are. They are very extensive, and a great obligation is put, not only upon the chair-main, but on the other two commissioners. The point I make has not been answered in this debate, and I intend that it shall be before this measure goes through. What I contend is that the government have changed their policy. This afternoon the Prime Minister claimed credit for what he is doing to-day. But what he is doing to-day is reversing the policy for which he claimed credit and which he presented to the people not long ago for their endorsation. We were to have a tribunal competent to deal with all these disputes between railway companies and the people, and that tribunal was to be responsible to government and to parliament. Now, however, that the elections are over, and when the public expect the government to carry out its pledges, we are told that the chairman of this commission is to be irresponsible. Until the point I make is answered, this legislation shall not go through. It may be six months before this session is over, or before the consent of the Governor General can be had to this legislation, and as far as I can gather the gentleman named may not be prepared to take the position until this measure becomes law. Is this commission to remain for months unmanned, and those questions left unsettled with which it was appointed to deal ?

Now, my charge is not that made by the hon. member for St. John city and county (Mr. Stockton) that this thing is wrong because it does not apply to all cases. 'My charge is that this is a reversal of policy. I protest against that reversal and against making the chairman of the commission an *officer not responsible to the Governor in Council, so that we may criticise the government for his acts, as we criticise any other acts of the ministers. Instead of having a commission simple in its methods, quick in its action, and one that can sit in any part of the country, we are to have a court whose presiding officer is not responsible to the administration. That is the charge that I want answered. I do not raise the smaller issues raised by the hon. gentleman (Mr. 'Stockton) [DOT]-if he will pardon me for so speaking. It is the complete reversal of policy, the setting at naught of the promises that were made two years ago, when this commission was established, when Hon. Mr. Blair, as shown by the record, declared that it would not do to have the chairman of the commission removable only by the cumbersome method of a joint address of both Houses of parliament. It is impossible, practically, to enforce such a means of responsibility. Suppose that a general election were being held which turned upon the administration of the law by this Railway Commission. It would be pleaded that the government was not responsible. And, if attempt were made to act through parliament, this doctrine of vested rights would be pleaded against any change in the policy of the commission. This is not the policy that was adopted when this commission was provided for by statute. The policy of that time is completely reversed. I do not care so much, for my part, for an explanation of these petty matters as to one man being treated differently from another, because he has been a judge ; it is the reversal of policy that I want explained. Still, as was pointed out by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Foster) there is an invidious distinction-a rule is made to apply to the chairman of the commission that does not apply to his colleagues. If the chairman is to be removed only upon joint address of the House of Commons and the Senate, why should not the same rule apply to the other members of the commission ? The argument used is that this is a special case. But what I object is that the government are using this special case to make a bad general rule. Under the law as it is, if the chairman of the Railway Commission is not doing his duty, that can be pointed out in this House, and an explanation demanded of the government.	The law provides that the
chairman may do this and shall do that ; but there is no clause of the law compelling the fulfilment of his duty, and it is left for this House, by holding the administration responsible to cause them to compel him to do his duty. And that is the great trouble with the laws we make.

We see it cropping up every day. No penalties are imposed and obligations are not fulfilled. The only course is this cumbrous and ineffective course of removal upon address of both Houses of parliament. I ask Ike government to explain the reason for its reversal of policy and the destruction of the usefulness of this great commission.

I was not here when the policy was laid down. I hope it is not going to take three months to go through with what we are doing in the matter. I certainly shall not be one to prolong the discussion. The case of Sir Robert Collier has been brought before the House by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick). That case does not apply. The law there was that a man could not be appointed to the judicial committee of the Privy Council unless he held high judical office. To comply with the letter of the law, they made him a judge, and two days afterwards appointed him to the judical committee. It was practically a device to permit an evasion of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What about the chief justice V

Lord Alverstone was master of the rolls. I am not talking about that case, and probably would not go as far as the Minister of Justice has stated with regard to it. Now, the chairman of the Railway Commission is essentially a judge, and we must recognize that fact. It may be a small matter, as my hon. friend (Mr. IV. F. Maclean) suggests, but I can see no objection'to making him as independent of the government of the day as is the chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada. But, suppose the first minister were to recommend the Minister of Justice as chairman of the Railway Commission. Under section 8, thte Minister of Justice, after being so appointed, could be dismissed from his office by order of the Governor in Council, because he holds no high judicial office. Why put a judge in a better position than the Minister of Justice would be if he were appointed ? It is an invidious distinction, and therefore, I say, it is special legislation. I hope the Minister of Justice will make it general, if it is the policy of the government, and make it apply to the chairman of the commission no matter what his office before appointment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Stockton), of course, sees at once the difference between my appointment-which, of course, is impossible-
It was only an illustration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, but even taking it as a matter of illustration-I have no acquired right to a retired allowance or to the position I occupy. But if you go to a judge and ask him to accept this position lie is well entitled to say : Why should you make my position more precarious under

the new appointment than it is at the present time ?

You can provide in the law that, it he is removed, he is to have a retiring allowance. You can make it a general law. I state to the Minister of Justice and to the members of this House that, as far as possible, all laws should be of general application.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is of general application with respect to a class of persons.
It is a general law made to suit a particular case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Stockton), I am sure will be willing to take a reasonable view of my difficulties, and will appreciate them, when he considers what fell from the lips of my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) and what fell from the lips of my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr Foster). In the one case I was asked to make a special law for this particular individual ; on the other hand I am told not to do any thing of the sort in any direction or in any case.
Well, I think it would be better legislation to make a special law for this particular case, which will just fit Ju'dge Killam, if he is to be the man ; and then after that, have the law general.

I object absolutely to that. I want what was promised to the people of this country, and I will insist on it, I want the chairman of that commission to be a responsible officer, under the doctrine of responsible government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will my hon. friend define what he means by responsibility ?

How does my hon. friend wish the commissioner to be responsible ? What does he mean by saying the commissioner is not going to be responsible ? Does he mean that he is not responsible to parliament or to the government ?
He is not responsible-using the words of hon. gentlemen opposite to the Governor in Council.
Do I understand him to wish that the resolution shall make the commissioner responsible to the Governor in Council ?
I wish the law to remain as it is. [DOT]
But what is the law ?
The hon. gentleman must read it for himself, he is a lawyer.
I am putting the question in all fairness, I am asking what is it he wishes.
I wish the law to remain as it is.
That the commissioner shall be responsible to the Governor General ?
As the Lieutenant Governor is, to use the words of those who introduced this Bill.

I want to know what the hon. gentleman means ?
Mr. \V. F. MACLEAN. I have told you very plainly. Again I say that the amendment changes the law. Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Belcourt) not remember that we on this side of the House have all been warned off : Don't touch this legislation ? They now propose to reverse the policy, and why ? Something has gone wrong, they have had a bad experience with their first appointee, and that chairman has done something that he should not have done. He left the whole court in a mess-if I may use the term. The legislation that should have been introduced here to-day was legislation which would prevent the recurrence of such a thing, and there ought to be some kind of provision in the law that the man who accepts the high position as chairman of that commission cannot leave it as this chairman has done. The chances are that we are to have no railway commission for three months, until this legislation can get through, and possibly it will be three months before the government's consent can be had. In the meantime the country will be tied up, and in the meantime the great expenses of this commission, $50,000 to $100,000 will continue, and the car which the commission procured because they could not wait to have one built in Canada, is lying sidetracked now, I suppose. There is no administration of that law, and there is a complete change in the policy. Again X ask the right hon. gentleman why this reversion of policy.
Section 8 of the Act says it is a court of record.
It also says it is a railway commission.

It is amusing to hear the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean), who is in his own estimation the champion of the people, taking the position he does to-night. As I understand it, the resolution will have the effect of making the chairman of the Railway Commission responsible to the two Houses of parliament. What my hon. friend wants now is to make him responsible to the Governor in Council only. Now, if that is consistent with the course which the hon. gentleman ever advocates in this House, and in his paper, he, the great champion of the people, I cannot understand his position. It is not consistent with his past, it is not consistent with the ideas which he constantly advocates.
The inconsistency is over there.

What does the hon. gentleman mean by saying that the chairman of the commission is not going to be responsible ? It means that according to him he won't be responsible to the Governor General. But by this resolution yon are going to make the chairman responsible to the whole country.
'MACLEAN. I want him responsible to the people directly.

You are going to make the chairman responsible to the advisers of His Majesty, they all being responsible directly to the people of Canada, of whom the hon. gentleman constitutes himself the champion. You are going to the highest court in the land, the parliament of Canada. Surely the hon. gentleman will see how absurd and how inconsistent his position is.
If the hon. gentleman will lecture those on his own side he will be consistent.

I hope the Minister of Justice will take the suggestion that has been made by my hon. friend from the county of St. John (Mr. Stockton). Perhaps the Minister of Justice will give me his view as to consistency in this respect. Did the minister make this first clause with this purpose in view, that as the chairman of the Railway Commission was a judicial officer, occupying the place of a judge quoad his jurisdiction in the matters that came before him, he thought he ought to be placed as a judge in the matter of dismissal ? Now if there is any principle underlying this Bill at all so far as the first section is concerned, that is the principle, there can be no other.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, that is not the principle.

Then there is no principle in the Bill. :It is simply a piece of special legislation made to fit the case of the present selection for appointment. So far as this Bill goes, it asserts that the chairman of the commission being a judge, occupying | the position of judge, it is best that he * should have the protection of a judge, that ; is, he should not be liable to be dismissed ! by Governor in Council, but he should have . the same security as a judge in that respect.
,	and	could	only be displaced	by parlia-
. ment acting* together. That is declared a . good thing to have for the sake of the com-i mission itself, as applied to the chairman.
, To be consistent you are bound to apply '	the	same	to every person	who, from
l	time to time, may be the chairman
.	acting as	a judge on that	commission.
Now then if that be the principle of your legislation, and if that is not the prin

 ciple there does not seem to be any principle at all, wli.v do you confine it simply to the

gentleman who is to be appointed in this case ? Why do you not hare the same general safety and security of tenure of office for every chairman of the commission who must be from the duties imposed upon him, acting as a judge ? If you do not take that ground, what ground will you take ? You may take the position, as I stated at first, that you are not making- legislation on principle, that you have a special case on hand, that you want a special man and that you cannot get him unless you put this legislation on the statute-book. If you come to that, then make it special entirely, and have it for this gentleman alone, but, leaving aside the difference of opinion that there may be as to whether the Governor in Council should have the power of dismissal or whether it should be parliament-we will not discuss that-if the government is of opinion that parliament should have this authority for the reasons which the hon. gentleman has given, then make it general so that it will apply to every chairman of the Railway Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The position which my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) has taken, as I understand it is this :	The chairman of
the commission, is by reason of the duties assigned to him under the Railway Act, a judge to all intents and purposes. Therefore, if he be a judge why not give to that gentleman who performs the duties of a judge the same fixity of tenure in office that a judge ought to have. There is a great deal to be said in favour of that, but that is not the view that is entertained by the government and that is not the object we have in view in proposing this resolution. If we had that object in view our resolution would fall absolutely short of our object. Our view is that we should open the door and extend the field of selection, that instead of being limited practically to a choice from laymen, as distinguishing them from judges, we should have the right to go to the judicial bench if we think it necessary in order to get a man for this office and we say that in order to get a man from the judicial bench we must take into account the conditions under which he fills his present office, and that if we wish to remove him from his present sphere to that other position we want to be in a position to tell him that as a result of the transfer from one place to another his present fixity of tenure shall not be interfered with.
What is there to prevent you from doing that with a chairman who is not a judge ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We*do not think it necessary because the chairman who is not a judge accepts the conditions as they exist. He accepts or he refuses. If he accepts he is not in any way interfered with in any right which he possesses at the time, because he has no office, but the other man has
been placed in a more difficult position. He would be asked to accept conditions which entail forfeiture of a right which he already possesses and it is to prevent that that we want this legislation. It may be that we are not at one on this. We undoubtedly do not agree. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Stockton) takes the position that this ought to be made general legislation. We take the position that it should be made legislation not applicable to the individual, but applicable to a class of individuals.
I have not yet had an answer to the question which I asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not try to give an answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean). I was speaking in answer to the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Foster).

This legislation, it is clear to me, is an attempt to destroy the usefulness of this commission. We were promised a responsible chairman of the commission, we are now to get an irresponsible chairman and once started the series will bo continued. There will never hereafter be a chairman of the commission who is responsible to the Governor in Council and whose conduct can with effect be discussed on the floor of this House. I am going to sit here and urge that the policy originally adopted should not be abandoned but that the chairman should be responsible to parliament directly through the Governor in Council, and that his conduct should be discussed in this House.
*. On resolution 2 :
Resolved, That if any chief commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, having been at the time of his appointment as such chief commissioner a judge of any Superior Court in Canada, or having resigned his office as such judge for the purpose of accepting appointment as such chief commissioner, has continued in office as judge of one or more Superior Courts in Canada and in the said office of chief commissioner for periods amounting together to fifteen years or upwards, or has become afflicted with a permanent infirmity disabling him from the due execution of his office, and if such chief commissioner resigns his office, or if his term of office, or any renewed term of office, has expired, His Majesty may, hy letters patent under the Great Seal, reciting such periods of office or such permanent infirmity, grant to such chief commissioner an annuity equal to two-thirds of the salary of the judicial office which he held at the time of his appointment as such chief commissioner, or which he resigned for the purpose of accepting such appointment, to commence immediately after his so ceasing to hold office as such chief commissioner, to continue thenceforth during his natural life, and to he payable by monthly instalments and pro rata for any period less than a year during such continuance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That resolution merely makes applicable to the chairman of the Railwaj' Commission that which is now

lapplicable to a judge ; that is to say that at the expiration of fifteen years he shall retire if he chooses on two-thirds of his allowance.

I have not examined that resolution with any care nor do I suppose I am capable of examining it without a good deal of trouble, but I would ask the hon. Minister of Justice if this section simply secures to the judges the retiring allowance which he should have if he remained a judge.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is it :
On resolution 3,
Resolved, That if any such chief commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners resigns his office or completes his term of service, original or renewed, therein, having, in either such case,
(a.) attained the age of seventy-five years, and continued in office as such judge and in the said office of chief commissioner for periods amounting together to twenty years or upwards, or	,
(b.) attained the age of seventy years, and continued in office as such judge and in the said office of chief commissioner for periods amounting together to twenty-five years or upwards, or
(c.) continued in office as such judge and in the said office of chief commissioner for periods amounting together to thirty years or upwards,
His Majesty may, by letters patent under the Great Seal-, reciting such period of service, and, in cases (a) and (b), such chief commissioner's age, grant to him an annuity, payable as aforesaid, equal to the salary of the judicial office which he held at the time of his appointment as such chief commissioner, or which he resigned for the purpose of accepting such appointment, to commence immediately after his resignation as chief commissioner and to continue thenceforth during his natural life.
What does this do ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This resolution is intended to cover the ease that was provided i'or by the statute of two years ago ; that is to say that a judge who has been thirty years on the bench, whatever may be his age, has the right to retire with full salary. If he is 75 years of age and has served 20 years he has also the right to retire with full salary, and if he is 70 years of age and has served 25 years on the bench he has also the right to retire with full salary.
All these are conditions that apply to judges as enacted a couple of years ago ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, except resolution No. 4.
If there is an increase in the salary he gets the benefit of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Exactly, that is No.
4.	We have not read that yet.
On resolution No. 4,
Resolved, That if between the date of the appointment of any such chief commissioner or of his resignation of his office as such judge and Mr. FITZPATRICK.
the date of his resignation of, or retirement from, the office of chief commissioner, the salary attached to the judicial office -which he held at the time of his appointment, or which he resigned for the purpose of accepting appointment as such chief commissioner, has been increased, the annuity to be granted to him hereunder may be increased in the same proportion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is to provide that in the event of an increase in salarybeing given to the judges between the appointment to the chairmanship of the Railway Commission and the time of retirement therefrom, the judge who happens to be the chairman of the Railway Commission gets the benefit of the increase yvith respect to retiring allowance.
Do you not think it is good enough now ?

I am always disposed to be good enough to the judges, but having-regard to the fact that the judge or chief justice who takes the position steps from a salary of $7,000 to $10,000, or some such figures, I think that this clause is unnecessary.
Mr. FOSTER, You are drawing it pretty fine there. I think the government capitulated.

I think we are now doing more than we should for the judges bygiving them their full allowance when superannuated, and I think it is going too far to do this. A man getting $7,000 a year and stepping into a position at $10,000 a year, if he holds that position for ten years has an increase of $30,000, and I think he might be well satisfied with that. I am against superannuation when it comes out of the pockets of the working people-the taxpayers of this country. There does not seem to be any inclination on the part of the government to take into account the people who pay the taxes. They seem to be anxious to heap more honours and pay on the officials. I am willing to have the officials well paid, but after you pay them for the services they render the country, I do not think you should provide for them in their old age. All people in the ordinary walks of life have to provide for their own old age, and I do not see why they should iu addition have to make provision for the old age of other people. I would ask to have clause 4 struck out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The intention of the legislation is that the judge, after he leaves his present position and goes on the Railway Commission, should continue to enjoy all the advantages which will attach to his present office if he continued in it, and this would be one of the benefits.

You must remember that you are giving him $3,000 a year more for the actual time spent in the service of his country. If he gets a superannuation

allowance of $7,000, is not that enough without adding any increase that may take place in the judges' salaries ? I might say that personally I think the judges are sufficiently paid now. I believe that the same kind of men would get the judgeships if you were to pay $10,000 as now get them, because it appears that no matter which party is in power the men who have the pull get the positions, and if a man is a kicker he is more apt to get a position whether he is fitted for it or not. As I stated last year, we had a vacancy in my own county, and any lawyer would have taken it at the present salary, but there is a continual desire on the part of the lawyers in this House to advocate an increased salary for the judges. A session or two ago we authorized the superannuation of judges on full pay. To my mind the whole thing was wrong, and it seems to me that if the people understood it fully, those members who voted for it would not again be elected. I may say that I think it helped me in my election. I had a majority three or four times what I had before, because I tried to explain the wrong-doings of this government.

I am sorry to hear my hon. friend (Mr. Wilson) speak as he has done about lawyers. I have noticed on many occasions that lawyers are made the butts of remarks that are not deserved.
Mr. FOSTER, They get revenge when it comes to fees.

I must say that, although there may be some justice in what the hon. gentleman says in some instances, it was not the prevailing rule when this was discussed before, that lawyers advocated large salaries for judges. They took occasion to point out that certain improvements were required in the judiciary, in the actions of some of the judges, &c., and perhaps these remarks were well founded. I also noticed that some gentlemen remarked this afternoon that the lawyers get the best of everything. I do not think they do in this world, although I think they will hereafter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not the popular belief, unfortunately.

Probably not. However, I do not think I succeeded in making myself understood a few moments ago. By the resolutions down to No. 4 we provide for what I think we might, in a general way, speak of as vested rights. We have made specific provision for the judges, and I think it is perfectly fair that a judge taking this position should not be deprived of any of the conditions existing at the present time for which we make provision, and in applying that rule to the circumstances with which we are dealing, I think that if a judge accepts the position of chairman of this commission he will be bettering himself by the addition of $3,000 a year to his salary dur-19
ing such time as he occupies the position, let us say, in round numbers, ten years. He is accepting a certainty, and is getting more than that ; he is getting also the contingencies in connection with the appointment to the new position, that is, if it should be found-and I do not think that this is beyond the range of possibility-that the position of chairman of the Railway Commission is a particularly onerous one, involving hard work-and I believe it will involve hard work-it may happen that we will raise the salary to even a higher point than it is to-day. He has that possibility in connection with the new position that he takes, and I submit that it is not fair to the people of this country, whom we represent, to give him the double possibility of an increase in his present salary and also of an increased retiring allowance due to the fact that the judges' salaries are raised because they are working hard in the services of their country. I do not see any justice in this. He is taking a hew position with a definite increase of $3,000 a year, and he has the possibility of an increase in salary, and I do not see any fair-play in saying that he should also have the possibility of benefiting from an increase in the judges' salaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If he retains his present office and an increase takes place in the judges' salaries-
How much ? Let us suppose a case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Say $2,000 to $9,000. If he retains his present position there are advantages connected with it which he would not enjoy as chairman of the Railway Commission. A judge of the Supreme Court would occupy an entirely different position with respect to judicial functions than the chairman of the Railway Commission ; he would not be obliged to go all over the country, as the chairman of the Railway Commission will in the exercise of his duty.
In a palace car.
With everything furnished, coloured porter, and all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are getting down to details now. If he remained on the bench, he would be entitled to the increase if any increase comes. If no increase comes, nobody suffers ; but if an increase comes, why should he not get the benefit of it ?
Because he gets a better office.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not a better office, the position of a judge of the Supreme Court is a very fine office.

It is a very fine office, but why should he get the benefit of an increase of salary that may be given to the judges of the Supreme Court after he has left the



bench and has got another position in which he gets 83,000 a year more salary. While on my feet I may say that X am opposed altogether to the way the commission is constituted. I would like to see it composed, as was originally intended of one railway expert, one lawyer, and X should hope the whole three men of common sense. Then, I think questions of law should not he left to the chairman alone, but should be argued before the whole three as before a jury, and let the three men decide. It seems to me that the three men are more likely to do justice. What we want above all is to have men of common sense and business men on the commission. I am opposed to this gentleman getting the benefit of any increase to the salaries of the judges after he has left the bench.
Suppose the salary were raised from $7,000 to $9,000, he would then get the superannuation on the additional $2,000 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He would get a superannuation on the basis of $9,000.

It is apparent, of course, to all of us that from the time he takes this office he gets $3,000 per year more than lie is getting now ; he gets far and away more than he could lose by any stoppage of an increased superannuation allowance which would result from a problematical or actual rise of $2,000 in salary. The government capitulated on all other points ; I do not think there was any need of their I capitulating on this point; and when you come down to the hard facts of the case, and face the men who have to pay the monev, however much these officials are paid, ' it is pretty hard to justify before them that you should give this man $30,000 extra during the subsistence of his office, and that he then should insist, and the government should go so far as to comply, that he should have the extra advantage, whatever it amounts to, of whatever rise of judges' salary there might be afterwards. All the contingencies that might be against him are provided for ; and if the country comes to believe, in the course of five years that $10,000 is not sufficient salary, he is not debarred from getting the larger salary which the country may think he shall get as chairman of the commission. $30,000 may be a slight matter for the minister but for myself, and to the taxpayers it is a very large amount, and I am opposed to that resolution 4, and I shall vote dead against it.
Resolution 4 agreed to.
Resolution 5 dropped.

I want to ask the Minister of Justice a question which I think is important. As I understand from an answer of the Prime Minister to a question the other day, it so happens that when the
chairman of the commission is not able to sit with his brother commissioners and decide cases which have been heard previously by them, for any reason, such as death or sudden vacation of office, all these cases fall to the ground, and have to be gone over again. Is that so ? If it is, it is a great hardship.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think my hon. friend has stated the case in too general terms.

If certain contingencies would make all the evidence which has been taken practically useless, the trouble is not so much the cost of taking the evidence over again as the fact that there is delay in remedying grievances, and life and property in the meantime are at stake. Does the government intend to make any provision for that ? You have a man leaving an office of trust, as was said to-day, in the twinkling of an eye, saying, as it were, ' I do not care how many lives may be risked at dangerous crossings or how much property may be endangered, my own interest is involved now, and I will let the people's interest go.' If a man can leave the commission so quickly and on so slight grounds, or if death intervenes and he is taken away suddenly, there should be a saving clause somewhere to provide that the result of the previous evidence shall be saved and that the grievance shall be quickly remedied.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As my hon. friend is aware, any two commissioners constitute a quorum. The difficulty arises from the fact that in some cases the evidence was taken before two commissioners one of whom disappeared. The other, who had not heard the evidence, could not act with the commissioner who had for the purpose of deciding the case. That difficulty occurs in courts of law every day.
Could not that be remedied by having the evidence taken down by a shorthand writer, so that the incoming commissioner could read it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am willing to consider that.
You could not have that without legislation. .

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would require that. The difficulty was that two commissioners went away and took evidence in the cases that came before them, and after they came back one of them resigned. The question was put before the Department of Justice whether the commissioner who had not sat and heard the evidence could under the statute take up the cases and deicde them. Of course, there was nothing for us under the statute except to say that the commissioner who had not heard the evidence was not competent to decide the

case. The question is whether it is not possible to put something in the statute to meet that difficulty. That is a question that may fairly be considered. There are some cases that will require to be re-heard, all of which happened in the Northwest Territories. The evidence is all typewritten, but the difficulty is that one of the commissioners has not seen the witnesses or visited the localities.

That could be overcome by statute. There is another question I would like to ask the minister. That statute provides that as regards questions of fact all the commissioners are judges, but that there is only one judge on questions of law, and that judge was the commissioner who resigned. In other words the legal gentleman is to be sole judge on questions of law. But as regards cases which turn upon a point of law-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not thought of that difficulty.
There is no way probably of getting over that difficulty because the sole judge of that particular point of the case has gone.
Before the resolutions are reported, will not the Minister of Justice give the committee the reasons assigned by the chairman for his hasty flight from that office.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I now say, in the presence of the Prime Minister and with his authority, that not one member of the government had any knowledge of the intention of the commissioner to resign, and that the only information we had is that contained in his telegram to the First Minister, in which he said that he had resigned the office. It was naturally expected that in the interval, because some days elapsed before his resignation was accepted, he would do something towards disposing of the arrears. The telegram was sent the 18th October, 1904, and his resignation was accepted the 31st October, 1904.
Have you the telegram ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, I have not got it here.
There was no explanation by him why he resigned ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Absolutely none. So far as the members of the government are concerned, his resignation came like a bolt from the blue, absolutely' without any notice.
That is an answer certainly and the House was entitled to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I ought to have given it at the beginning and I had it in my notes to give it. My right hon. friend, the 19*
Prime Minister, is prepared to bring down the telegram and lay it on the table.
Resolutions reported, read the second time and agreed to.

speechtext: I must ask my hon. friend to make a motion.

For copies of all correspondence between the government or any minister, and any party or parties, concerning the dismissal of the postmaster at Shelburne, Ontario, on or about the 7th of March, 1903.
He said : My object is to ascertain why the postmaster was dismissed. In order that the House may understand the position, I need only refer to the history of the case. In 1867 Mr. Berwick was appointed postmaster at the village of Shelburne, Out., and during 37 years, up to the year 1903, he filled that position with credit to himself and to the entire satisfaction of the community. He continued to occupy that position, not only during the time of the Conservative government, but also under the Mackenzie government, and there never was any complaint made against him. It is true that Mr. Berwick is a partner in a mercantile firm at Shelburne-one of these partners-and probably did employ some of his time in looking after the interests of his business. But during the distribution of Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
mail matter he was almost always at his post and at all times he had an efficient assistant, quite competent to attend to the business should Mr. Berwick ever happen to be away. The best proof of the manner in which he conducted the post office is to be found in the fact that during all those years no complaint was made against him, until the year 1903 when, I understand, the charge was made that he had other business outside to attend to, and that there were good reformers who had not any business to look after, and who consequently should be looked after by the government. That I believe was the real cause of Mr. Berwick's dismissal. It may no doubt be charged that he was not always in the post office, but we must remember that Shelburne is but a village, and there are few village postmasters who are in their office the whole time. If they have an efficient assistant, that" is considered quite sufficient, and I venture to say that the postmaster who is now at Shelburne is not more often in his place than was the late postmaster and probably has not as efficient an assistant.
But, early in 1903, an agitation was got up by a few-probably not more than a baker's dozen-every one of whom was an applicant for the office-to have a change made. And when the change was made and the new appointment settled, I venture to say the dozen agitators who had failed were just as much dissatisfied with the change as were any others in that village. So I do not think the government will gain any friends by the change. The agitation was carried on beneath the surface. No petition, so far as we knew, was circulated. The majority of the people using the office neither made nor heard of any complaint. But those who were anxious to obtain the office, gained the assistance of a senator, and probably of a member of the House, although both are outside of the riding and have no interest in the matter whatever except in promoting the welfare of their friends in the reform party ; now could they have had any object in removing the postmaster who had grown gray in that service ? And they succeeded in bringing about the change without the member then representing the county, without 99 out of a hundred of the people really interested knowing anything about it. Mr. Berwick had held the office for thirty-seven years was replaced without any reason given, so far as I know. No just cause was assigned- there was none to assign. These agitators succeeded in putting one of their party friends in the place that Mr. Berwick had occupied so long. Now, Mr. Speaker, if we are to have the American system adopted in Canada, the course taken by hon. gentlemen opposite in this matter is the one that is most likely to bring it about. It is well known that in all the various departments, this government are weeding out the Con' servatives, so that in the very near future

not a Conservative will be left in the public service of the Dominion. But I wish to remind hon. gentlemen opposite of the signs of the times. They cannot shut their eyes to the fact that one province after another is going Conservative by overwhelming majorities-the latest by a perfect landslide. If the incoming government in Ontario were to follow the example of the hon. gentlemen opposite there would be a weeding out of officers that have not attended to their duties; and if they were to follow it completely, even men who had attended to their duties, as Mr. Edward Berwick did, would be dismissed on some excuse to make way for friends of the party in power. We have only to follow the example set by this government to have the spoils system established in this province. In my opinion, it was an evil day for this Dominion when that system was inaugurated ; but the government cannot blame Conservatives if the Liberals in Ontario are given a dose of their own medicine in the near future. We have no desire to follow that course ; we should regret to be driven to it ; but we cannot be blamed for following it, if it aifords the only means by which we can protect our own friends. I know that the cry may be raised that Mr. Berwick had an interest in a store in Shelburne. But it cannot he shown that he in any way neglected the duties of the post office. As I have stated he was in his place day by day when the mail was delivered, and there was nothing in what he did to afford just ground for complaint. When the papers come down, I hope we shall learn who was the power behind the throne in causing the removal of Mr. Berwick without the member for the county or the great body of the people interested having any knowledge of what was going on.
Hon. Sir WILLIAM MULOCK-(Postmaster General)-There can be no objection to the order going. I think that when it is obeyed and the papers are brought down, it will appear that the change of postmaster to which my hon. friend (Mr. Barr) refers was not brought about by any political considerations. I think the hon. gentleman himself has given the explanation. I should infer, from his own admission that the reason for the change was that the postmastership at Shelburne had attained such importance as to entitle it to the undivided services of the person holding it. I speak now without any recollection of the facts. Perhaps I ought to apologize for not having informed myself ; but I failed to notice the motion on the paper in time. I have sent for the papers in the case, and had hoped that they would arrive before I needed to make my remarks. .However, the lion gentleman from Dufferin (Mr. Barr) himself has stated that the village of Shelburne has grown a place of considerable importance. I presume that there are many merchants there competitors in business of the gentleman wno held the postmastership. If such are the facts, I think it will be made clear by the papers in this case, when they are produced, that the change has been made in pursuance of the policy of the department that the postmastership of a place shall not be held by a person engaged in other business if the office itself furnishes sufficient emoluments to give the officer a living about on a par with the average earnings of the people there. You can well understand, Mr. Speaker, how a village postmaster who is carrying on the business of a general store has, by reason of his office, special advantages over his rivals. As long as the revenue is not sufficient to furnish a good living for the postmaster, that condition of affairs is not disturbed. But when the place grows in importance, and exception is taken to it by competitors, some attention must be paid to those objections. I think my hon. friend will find such to be the conditions in this case. I do not dwell upon his other statement, nor would I regard it as a sufficient reason for a change that this gentleman had held the office for thirty-seven years. A man who has held an office for thirty-seven years has been fairly successful. If it was only in 1903 that he was disturbed by this government,
I think there was no undue haste to disturb him. After he had been for thirty-seven years in the enjoyment of that office, I have no doubt any action that was taken was for the reason that I have assigned, not on account of any political considerations.

If I may be allowed to reply -I regret the Postmaster General did not see fit to ask me to allow the motion to stand so that he might get information that would throw more light upon it. The very fact, as the hon. gentleman says, that a man had been thirty-seven years in the position, was sufficient to remove him
I did not make that statement.

man able to tell ns that any petition came in against this postmaster. [DOT] There may have been, but if so, the petitions were sent in without the knowledge of the free and independent electors there, and had they known it a contrary petition would have been sent in signed by a great many Reformers as well as Conservatives. I think I have given the true solution, namely, that he was engaged in business and had a partner in the store. Well, Mr. Speaker, you know that in small places like that postmasters often have other business, the post office business is so small that it does not occupy much of their time, and it frequently happens that they employ competent men to assist them.' I say again, I regret that the hon. gentleman, finding himself unable to give the information, did not allow the motion to stand, because I would have been able to enlighten him on many points. His friends probably misled him. I think possibly he would not have made the change had he been cognizant of all the facts.
I think my hon. friend would have done well to reserve his judgment. When he receives the papers I think he will have occasion to change his views. A large number of his own friends asked for it.
Motion agreed to.
